Chris Bertish - nothing is impossible!

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
He has surfed death defying waves, paddled 4000 miles across the Atlantic and is now embarking on his next crazy adventure. We visit the man behind these crazy dreams.

Unique Selling Point:
Chris Bertish, international speaker, author, conservationist and award-winning waterman, is a man driven by passion: passion for the ocean and those in need who he helps through charitable organizations. When he sets his mind to something, there is no stopping Bertish. He relentlessly pushes the boundaries of his own physical and mental strength to achieve what most people will say is impossible! And through this determination has set a number of world first records.


Summary:
Chris Bertish is no ordinary man. Driven by passion, and powered by purpose this 46 year old Cape Tonian learnt from his late father - an SA ski and canoe champ in his heyday - to brave the elements and take risks from a young age. His father introduced him to every kind of watersport and the love for the ocean. At a young age Bertish became an accomplished waterman beyond the borders of South Africa where he set a number of ‘world first’ records.

In 2010 he became the first South African big wave surfer to be invited to the prestigious Mavericks Big Wave event in Half Moon Bay, California in 2010. Surfing some of the biggest waves in history, he won!. In 2013-14 Bertish set three separate Stand Up Paddle World Records, two in Europe and the Open Ocean, 12-hour SUP Guinness World Distance Record. In 2015 he co-directed and released the acclaimed film Ocean Driven and launched the best-selling book Stoked! Both about his life story.

In 2017, Bertish redefined adventure by stand up paddling solo and unsupported across the Atlantic Ocean, over 4000 miles from Morocco to the Caribbean in 93 days, raising money for Operation Smile and the support of youth, education and ocean conservation initiatives.

The Transatlantic SUP Crossing won Bertish the global “Expedition of the Year Award” at the 2017 US Global SUP Awards and being named one of the Top-100 Genius Icons, by Global Genis 100, Leaders of Innovation and Creativity, by the Einstein Institute in 2018.

In June 2021 he planned to cross 2850 miles across the `Pacific Ocean from half Moon Bay, california to Oahu, Hawai in a would be first “solo, wing foil transpacific crossing” but due to technical issues had to put the project on hold till May next year.

In August this year he launched his second film, “Last Known Coordinates” about his epic Transatlantic stand up paddle journey.


Further information:
Bertish is planning his next big challenge for May 2022: to embark on a solo wing foil, 2,850 miles across the Pacific Ocean from Half Moon /BHay, California to Oahu, Hawaii with the goal of raising awareness and funding for charitable organisations that are navigating global challenges including climate change and poverty.

The Transpacific Wing Project craft was custom built for Bertish’s 2017 solo paddle journey across the Atlantic but has been update and significantly modified with the most advanced satellite communication system, radar, GPS, hydrofoils, and powerful wings which he will used to harness the wind to power his adventure across the Pacific. The journey will require Bertish to wing a minimum of 10-15 hours per day, for over sixty days straight, unsupported and completely unassisted. In June, only after five days into this journey, he was forced to turn around when he encountered technical problems on his craft. But as Bertish says, “it is not a failure. It has only shown me what needs to be done better.” The date is set for May next year when Bertish will attempt a world first, solo wing-foil ocean crossing relying entirely on the energy of the sun to once again raise awareness and inspire positive mind change.

“We are stronger than we realise, and if we set our sights on a goal and overcome a challenge, we can get through anything,” says Bertish. He is currently back in South Africa from the US for the launch of his second documentary, “Last Known Coordinates” - a film that captures the
epic Transatlantic stand up paddle journey.

The story: We will interview Bertish at their family home in Langebaan where we will also get some visuals of him on the stand-up board on the ocean and being in his old home environment again after years of traveling and staying in different parts of the world whilst getting ready for his various epic challenges. We will have visuals of his achievements and the epic journey across the Atlantic as well as some of the preparation shots for the Solo Wing-Foil Ocean crossing. We could also interview his middle brother, Conn, who will give a sense of the family unit and the close-knit unit the three brothers have formed over the years. His long-time friend, Andrew Hoeks who will talk about their friendship, his character as a ‘solid, caring and empathetic man’ and his ability to give back. Darren Robertson, the logistics and financial planner behind some of the projects will share his thoughts about the hair raising times they had in scraping together enough funds for Bertish to achieve his goals and juggling all the time to make it happen, because Bertish does not take no for an answer.

Although Carte Blanche covered the Maverick success and the run-up to the 2017 challenge, there is much more to talk about in this recap on Bertish’s life and his next goal and visuals to colour in the scenes.

Script: Chris Bertish - Nothing is impossible
8 Minutes

UP natural sound

Chris Bertish - Award-winning Waterman: I think this place, especially this house that we are in and Langebaan as a lagoon is pretty much all the memories that I can remember as fond times of growing up in and around the ocean and the lagoon and becoming comfortable with the ocean environment in every way, shape and form and I think that is what helped shape me.

V/O Chris Bertish is the ultimate waterman and comfortable on the ocean in any craft he sets his sights on. He has explored a life-time of adventures and cracked world-first records in adverse conditions that only a man of extreme courage and discipline would dream of. His love of the ocean was formed at a very young age.

Link: This is where the Bertish family spent most of their holidays in Langebaan on the Cape West Coast. The ocean and watersport were in their blood and for the youngest of the three sons, Chris, it was to become his life.

Chris Bertish: I was very fortunate to grow up the youngest of three naughty brothers and we spent a lot of time in the ocean. My dad was an amazing human, incredible waterman himself. He skied for Britain and South Africa and built the first ever catamaran just over here. We use to sail out here, ski out there, surf just by the lagoon. We just spent all our time immersed in the ocean and I think that is what really helped to create us into the very adventurous humans that we are.

V/O Nicknamed Chrispie, Chris worked extra hard to keep up with his older brothers Greg and Conn.

Conn Bertish - Brother: It was probably the classic younger kid who is trying to catch up and I was trying to catch up to my older brother Greg and I was kind of getting there but poor old Chrispie he had to try and catch up double. And in that dynamic he developed that incredible skill of discipline and that has enabled him to overcome all these different challenges that he put himself in because he is so disciplined Derek.

V/O Then suddenly his father died when Bertish was barely 21. It left a void he tried to fill by setting goals his father would have been proud of.

Chris Bertish: What I learnt from that is that he had given me such a great gift of being so comfortable in the ocean.

V/O Bertish was comfortable in most watersports but his ultimate goal was to become a big wave surfer. The Mavericks Big Wave event in California was his childhood dream.

Chris Bertish: Mavericks that was a pretty big deal because it was probably something that I was working on for 10 years, probably 15 years to become one of the best big wave surfers in the world.

Derek Watts: Describe catching that wave?

Chris Bertish: Catching a 60-foot wave which is equivalent to a 5-story building and then being at the top of that and having to commit. Everything slows down when the adrenaline kicks in and you’ve got to be really sure of yourself and sure you can make it out on the other side in one piece.

Derek Watts: Which not everybody has.

Chris Bertish: Not everybody has. A couple of friends that I have known have died, a couple of friends have died, especially at Mavericks.

V/O Bertish became the first South African to win the legendary Mavericks Big Wave event in 2010. From big wave surfing he turned to author and motivational speaker. Then breaking the 12-hour Guinness World record on a stand-up-paddle board was only a stepping stone for him, as he managed 8 days and 350km from Cape Point to Lambert’s Bay, unsupported.

Chris Bertish: I got to the point that I used all these different adventures, it is almost like stepping stones, ...everything was building blocks to go bigger.

Link: In 2017 Bertish embarked on his most ambitious and dangerous adventure: a mammoth quest to paddle solo, 4050 miles across the Atlantic ocean spending more than 3 months at sea unsupported.

V/O Bertish had a circle of close friends who were behind his every adventure. Andrew Hoeks was one of his surfing buddies.

Andrew Hoeks - Friend: I think I followed the grand total of all his exploits. As a friend it is my duty to have his back and get myself on his side when he needs support.

Derek Watts: He has been on many missions, dangerous ones but how did you feel about the Transatlantic Crossing?

Andrew Hoeks: I think at that point I thought he probably lost the plot.

V/O The voyage would take 93 days to paddle from Agadir Morocco to the Caribbean island of Antigua on a tiny vessel called Impi Fish. Behind the missionwas his drive to make a difference in the lives of other people and the planet. Funds raised would go to Operation Smile, education and ocean conservation initiatives which he felt passionate about.

Chris Bertish: I spent almost three-and-a-half to five years planning that journey, and designing and building the craft in the uk and then tweaking all these different elements that had never been done before for a craft that had never been built before.

V/O Darren Robertson, a friend from varsity days, was in charge of the logistics and financial planning.

Derek Watts: Now for a project like that you needed cash.

Darren Roberston - Friend: Absolutely. We basically never had enough money. Chris fundraised himself to death, we had good corporate sponsorship but budgets get blown out with time.

Derek Watts: When you said goodbye to him in Morocco did it cross your mind it might be for the last time?

Darren Robertson: Absolutely we actually discussed that. He was at peace with that.

V/O The Impi Fish was kitted with satellite and navigation systems and solar panels vital to keep the comms going. Food rations and medical supplies were carefully stored away in neat compartments.

Derek Watts: Chris if you paddle away on the Atlantic but you also have to be a manager. There are so many things to do aboard that craft?

Chris Bertish: And it is like project management 101 but 24/7, 7 days a week for 93 days. When I was not on deck and I was not paddling which was between 12 and 15 hours a day which is like doing a full iron man. You are still making your nutrition, making your hydration, making your water, looking out that you are not going to be run over by supertankers, getting eaten by great white sharks, fixing the leaks when I think I am going to sink.

UP sound: “I have lost all my water bottles, everything to drink out of”

Derek Watts: You said you were at your happiest when you were in the middle of the Atlantic?

Chris Bertish: I remember that moment when I was as far away from any other human on the planet. I was right in the middle of the Atlantic, 2000 miles to Africa, 2000 miles to North America. And I became so connected and comfortable with my environment. That’s very rare and a very special place to find within yourself.

V/O The solitude for days on end brought mixed feelings and at times the challenges to survive tested his mental capacity to the limit.

Up sound: “I have never been so desperate to try and finish something in my life!

V/O After more than 3 months on the ocean, the end was in sight and a support vessel was sent out in stormy seas to see if they could spot Bertish.

Chris Bertish: I think it was the first time they had actually seen and experienced what I had actually been dealing with what I had actually been doing for 93 days in that deadly ocean. It was a pretty iconic way to finish an incredible journey that day.

Link: And now Bertish is preparing for his next epic adventure, a solo journey across the Pacific Ocean, powered entirely by nature in what is called a ‘wing foil’.

V/O In May next year he plans to wing foil a record 2850 miles across the Pacific Ocean from California to Hawaii. It will be on his beloved Impi Fish - but this time with wings and powered entirely by nature. The goal of this project is to raise awareness and funding for charitable organisations and climate change.

Chris Bertish: I really believe we are being put on the planet to do something extraordinary and utilise your gifts whatever gifts you may have and give back to the world. I am utilising my gifts to hopefully inspire other people give back and make a positive impact on the world and other people around me.
_______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo one: 22 seconds
V/O Chris Bertish spent 5 years in preparation for an epic journey that would take him across the Atlantic Ocean 4050 miles and 93 days - unsupported he faced some of the worst weather conditions on a stand up paddle.
Chris Bertish: The point that you think you are not going to make it is when you give up and for me, I never give up.

Promo two: 22 seconds
V/O From a skinny little kid growing up in Cape Town and learning from his father to sail just about every type of craft, Chris Bertish proved that the ‘impossible’ can be done: paddling one stroke at a time across the wild Atlantic Ocean unsupported, reaching his destination after 93 grueling days.

Promo three: 11 seconds
V/O He surfed death defying waves and paddled solo 4050 miles across the Atlantic Ocean for 93 days. We meet the man behind these crazy dreams.

V/O Chris Bertish is the ultimate waterman and comfortable on the ocean in any craft he sets his sights on. He has explored a life-time of adventures and cracked world-first records in adverse conditions that only a man of extreme courage and discipline would dream of. His love of the ocean was formed at a very young age. Link: This is where the Bertish family spent most of their holidays in Langebaan on the Cape West Coast. The ocean and watersport were in their blood and for the youngest of the three sons, Chris, it was to become his life. Chris Bertish: I was very fortunate to grow up the youngest of three naughty brothers and we spent a lot of time in the ocean. My dad was an amazing human, incredible waterman himself. He skied for Britain and South Africa and built the first ever catamaran just over here. We use to sail out here, ski out there, surf just by the lagoon. We just spent all our time immersed in the ocean and I think that is what really helped to create us into the very adventurous humans that we are. V/O Nicknamed Chrispie, Chris worked extra hard to keep up with his older brothers Greg and Conn. Conn Bertish - Brother: It was probably the classic younger kid who is trying to catch up and I was trying to catch up to my older brother Greg and I was kind of getting there but poor old Chrispie he had to try and catch up double. And in that dynamic he developed that incredible skill of discipline and that has enabled him to overcome all these different challenges that he put himself in because he is so disciplined Derek. V/O Then suddenly his father died when Bertish was barely 21. It left a void he tried to fill by setting goals his father would have been proud of. Chris Bertish: What I learnt from that is that he had given me such a great gift of being so comfortable in the ocean. V/O Bertish was comfortable in most watersports but his ultimate goal was to become a big wave surfer. The Mavericks Big Wave event in California was his childhood dream. Chris Bertish: Mavericks that was a pretty big deal because it was probably something that I was working on for 10 years, probably 15 years to become one of the best big wave surfers in the world. Derek Watts: Describe catching that wave? Chris Bertish: Catching a 60-foot wave which is equivalent to a 5-story building and then being at the top of that and having to commit. Everything slows down when the adrenaline kicks in and you’ve got to be really sure of yourself and sure you can make it out on the other side in one piece. Derek Watts: Which not everybody has. Chris Bertish: Not everybody has. A couple of friends that I have known have died, a couple of friends have died, especially at Mavericks. V/O Bertish became the first South African to win the legendary Mavericks Big Wave event in 2010. From big wave surfing he turned to author and motivational speaker. Then breaking the 12-hour Guinness World record on a stand-up-paddle board was only a stepping stone for him, as he managed 8 days and 350km from Cape Point to Lambert’s Bay, unsupported. Chris Bertish: I got to the point that I used all these different adventures, it is almost like stepping stones, ...everything was building blocks to go bigger. Link: In 2017 Bertish embarked on his most ambitious and dangerous adventure: a mammoth quest to paddle solo, 4050 miles across the Atlantic ocean spending more than 3 months at sea unsupported. V/O Bertish had a circle of close friends who were behind his every adventure. Andrew Hoeks was one of his surfing buddies. Andrew Hoeks - Friend: I think I followed the grand total of all his exploits. As a friend it is my duty to have his back and get myself on his side when he needs support. Derek Watts: He has been on many missions, dangerous ones but how did you feel about the Transatlantic Crossing? Andrew Hoeks: I think at that point I thought he probably lost the plot. V/O The voyage would take 93 days to paddle from Agadir Morocco to the Caribbean island of Antigua on a tiny vessel called Impi Fish. Behind the missionwas his drive to make a difference in the lives of other people and the planet. Funds raised would go to Operation Smile, education and ocean conservation initiatives which he felt passionate about. Chris Bertish: I spent almost three-and-a-half to five years planning that journey, and designing and building the craft in the uk and then tweaking all these different elements that had never been done before for a craft that had never been built before. V/O Darren Robertson, a friend from varsity days, was in charge of the logistics and financial planning. Derek Watts: Now for a project like that you needed cash. Darren Roberston - Friend: Absolutely. We basically never had enough money. Chris fundraised himself to death, we had good corporate sponsorship but budgets get blown out with time. Derek Watts: When you said goodbye to him in Morocco did it cross your mind it might be for the last time? Darren Robertson: Absolutely we actually discussed that. He was at peace with that. V/O The Impi Fish was kitted with satellite and navigation systems and solar panels vital to keep the comms going. Food rations and medical supplies were carefully stored away in neat compartments. Derek Watts: Chris if you paddle away on the Atlantic but you also have to be a manager. There are so many things to do aboard that craft? Chris Bertish: And it is like project management 101 but 24/7, 7 days a week for 93 days. When I was not on deck and I was not paddling which was between 12 and 15 hours a day which is like doing a full iron man. You are still making your nutrition, making your hydration, making your water, looking out that you are not going to be run over by supertankers, getting eaten by great white sharks, fixing the leaks when I think I am going to sink. UP sound: “I have lost all my water bottles, everything to drink out of” Derek Watts: You said you were at your happiest when you were in the middle of the Atlantic? Chris Bertish: I remember that moment when I was as far away from any other human on the planet. I was right in the middle of the Atlantic, 2000 miles to Africa, 2000 miles to North America. And I became so connected and comfortable with my environment. That’s very rare and a very special place to find within yourself. V/O The solitude for days on end brought mixed feelings and at times the challenges to survive tested his mental capacity to the limit. Up sound: “I have never been so desperate to try and finish something in my life! V/O After more than 3 months on the ocean, the end was in sight and a support vessel was sent out in stormy seas to see if they could spot Bertish. Chris Bertish: I think it was the first time they had actually seen and experienced what I had actually been dealing with what I had actually been doing for 93 days in that deadly ocean. It was a pretty iconic way to finish an incredible journey that day. Link: And now Bertish is preparing for his next epic adventure, a solo journey across the Pacific Ocean, powered entirely by nature in what is called a ‘wing foil’. V/O In May next year he plans to wing foil a record 2850 miles across the Pacific Ocean from California to Hawaii. It will be on his beloved Impi Fish - but this time with wings and powered entirely by nature. The goal of this project is to raise awareness and funding for charitable organisations and climate change. Chris Bertish: I really believe we are being put on the planet to do something extraordinary and utilise your gifts whatever gifts you may have and give back to the world. I am utilising my gifts to hopefully inspire other people give back and make a positive impact on the world and other people around me. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo one: 22 seconds V/O Chris Bertish spent 5 years in preparation for an epic journey that would take him across the Atlantic Ocean 4050 miles and 93 days - unsupported he faced some of the worst weather conditions on a stand up paddle. Chris Bertish: The point that you think you are not going to make it is when you give up and for me, I never give up. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): He has surfed death defying waves, paddled 4000 miles across the Atlantic and is now embarking on his next crazy adventure. We visit the man behind these crazy dreams.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Chris Bertish, international speaker, author, conservationist and award-winning waterman, is a man driven by passion: passion for the ocean and those in need who he helps through charitable organizations. When he sets his mind to something, there is no stopping Bertish. He relentlessly pushes the boundaries of his own physical and mental strength to achieve what most people will say is impossible! And through this determination has set a number of world first records.
metadata.Summary: Chris Bertish is no ordinary man. Driven by passion, and powered by purpose this 46 year old Cape Tonian learnt from his late father - an SA ski and canoe champ in his heyday - to brave the elements and take risks from a young age. His father introduced him to every kind of watersport and the love for the ocean. At a young age Bertish became an accomplished waterman beyond the borders of South Africa where he set a number of ‘world first’ records. In 2010 he became the first South African big wave surfer to be invited to the prestigious Mavericks Big Wave event in Half Moon Bay, California in 2010. Surfing some of the biggest waves in history, he won!. In 2013-14 Bertish set three separate Stand Up Paddle World Records, two in Europe and the Open Ocean, 12-hour SUP Guinness World Distance Record. In 2015 he co-directed and released the acclaimed film Ocean Driven and launched the best-selling book Stoked! Both about his life story. In 2017, Bertish redefined adventure by stand up paddling solo and unsupported across the Atlantic Ocean, over 4000 miles from Morocco to the Caribbean in 93 days, raising money for Operation Smile and the support of youth, education and ocean conservation initiatives. The Transatlantic SUP Crossing won Bertish the global “Expedition of the Year Award” at the 2017 US Global SUP Awards and being named one of the Top-100 Genius Icons, by Global Genis 100, Leaders of Innovation and Creativity, by the Einstein Institute in 2018. In June 2021 he planned to cross 2850 miles across the `Pacific Ocean from half Moon Bay, california to Oahu, Hawai in a would be first “solo, wing foil transpacific crossing” but due to technical issues had to put the project on hold till May next year. In August this year he launched his second film, “Last Known Coordinates” about his epic Transatlantic stand up paddle journey.
metadata.Further information: Bertish is planning his next big challenge for May 2022: to embark on a solo wing foil, 2,850 miles across the Pacific Ocean from Half Moon /BHay, California to Oahu, Hawaii with the goal of raising awareness and funding for charitable organisations that are navigating global challenges including climate change and poverty. The Transpacific Wing Project craft was custom built for Bertish’s 2017 solo paddle journey across the Atlantic but has been update and significantly modified with the most advanced satellite communication system, radar, GPS, hydrofoils, and powerful wings which he will used to harness the wind to power his adventure across the Pacific. The journey will require Bertish to wing a minimum of 10-15 hours per day, for over sixty days straight, unsupported and completely unassisted. In June, only after five days into this journey, he was forced to turn around when he encountered technical problems on his craft. But as Bertish says, “it is not a failure. It has only shown me what needs to be done better.” The date is set for May next year when Bertish will attempt a world first, solo wing-foil ocean crossing relying entirely on the energy of the sun to once again raise awareness and inspire positive mind change. “We are stronger than we realise, and if we set our sights on a goal and overcome a challenge, we can get through anything,” says Bertish. He is currently back in South Africa from the US for the launch of his second documentary, “Last Known Coordinates” - a film that captures the epic Transatlantic stand up paddle journey. The story: We will interview Bertish at their family home in Langebaan where we will also get some visuals of him on the stand-up board on the ocean and being in his old home environment again after years of traveling and staying in different parts of the world whilst getting ready for his various epic challenges. We will have visuals of his achievements and the epic journey across the Atlantic as well as some of the preparation shots for the Solo Wing-Foil Ocean crossing. We could also interview his middle brother, Conn, who will give a sense of the family unit and the close-knit unit the three brothers have formed over the years. His long-time friend, Andrew Hoeks who will talk about their friendship, his character as a ‘solid, caring and empathetic man’ and his ability to give back. Darren Robertson, the logistics and financial planner behind some of the projects will share his thoughts about the hair raising times they had in scraping together enough funds for Bertish to achieve his goals and juggling all the time to make it happen, because Bertish does not take no for an answer. Although Carte Blanche covered the Maverick success and the run-up to the 2017 challenge, there is much more to talk about in this recap on Bertish’s life and his next goal and visuals to colour in the scenes.
